planting.note: Plant out after frost danger passes and mound extra mulch over the crown going into winter, since tops die back hard below the low 20s F but the roots resprout vigorously from colder snaps.

directions: This Ethiopian highland shrub carries wide, silvery-green leaves edged in soft spines and sends up spikes of bright orange-red flowers from summer into fall, a striking color break from the usual purple-flowered acanthus. Site it in sharply drained soil with full to part sun and treat it as drought tolerant once rooted in, though it takes occasional summer water without complaint. In the Pacific Northwest and similar zone 8 gardens expect the top growth to collapse in a hard freeze; cut back the dead stems in late winter and the roots will push fresh growth back vigorously once the ground warms.

subcategory: New Zealand alpine spiny tussock perennial

planting.note: Give nursery-grown starts a sheltered transition spot before moving them to a hot, exposed site, since container stock has been shielded from the intense sun and drying wind this tussock tolerates once established.

directions: Collected from New Zealand's high-elevation Pisa Range grasslands, this speargrass builds a dense, deer-resistant tussock of rigid, spine-tipped foliage that can eventually reach three feet across. Mature plants send up bold flower spikes two to three feet tall lined with spiny bracts and creamy-yellow blooms, giving the clump a sculptural second season of interest. Grow it in average, well-draining soil that stays evenly moist to dry, with full sun in cooler climates and afternoon shade where summers run hot, and be patient since alpine tussocks like this take several years to bulk up to flowering size.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall as growth begins, keep them in well-drained soil, and let the ground run dry through the following summer dormancy to avoid rot.

directions: This white-flowered selection of the South African Eastern Cape species sends up roughly foot-tall stems in late autumn topped with frilly, undulating-petaled flowers, with the strap-shaped leaves emerging around the same time. It is a winter grower that wants sun to light shade and reliably drained soil while in leaf, then a dry summer rest once the foliage dies back. Clumps slowly bulk up into dense colonies over the years, making it a good candidate for a trough, raised bed, or rock garden where its unusual fall bloom timing stands out against typical spring bulbs.

planting.note: Set divisions into lean, sharply drained soil in spring so roots establish before the first winter, since soggy lean soil in winter is more of a risk than cold itself.

directions: What sets this red hot poker apart from the usual garden torch lilies is its covering of stiff, hairy leaves, which keep the clump textural and interesting even when it is not in bloom. Two-foot flower stalks push up and open into the classic orange-red poker spikes, drawing hummingbirds through the season. It is noticeably hardier than many Kniphofia, taking temperatures down to around minus ten Fahrenheit, and prefers lean, well-drained soil over rich garden loam, so skip the extra compost and let it go dry between waterings once established.

planting.note: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil with shelter from cold wind, since this comes from shaded cliff faces in the Taiwanese mountains and resents both exposure and poor drainage.

directions: Collected from shady cliffs in the mountains of northeastern Taiwan, this evergreen euonymus starts out loose and sprawling as a young plant and gradually matures into a more structured shrub to around six feet, with elliptic leaves that enlarge with age. In fall it produces clusters of round seed capsules covered in odd curved spines, an unusual textural feature beyond the typical euonymus fruit. Grow it in sun to part shade in fertile, well-drained soil with protection from cold winter wind, treating it as a zone 8 plant, possibly hardier with a sheltered microclimate.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native evergreen huckleberry selection

planting.note: Mulch well at planting and give full sun near the coast but understory shade from larger shrubs or trees further inland, mirroring how it naturally performs in each setting.

directions: This Cistus Nursery introduction is a selected form of the West Coast native evergreen huckleberry, with an upright, congested branching habit and new leaves flushed orange before settling into dark evergreen. Light pink flowers in late winter and early spring give way to small purplish-black berries that are genuinely edible off the bush. It tolerates summer drought once rooted in but does not mind occasional water, and unlike some related huckleberries it handles the sterile, mineral soils typical of built landscapes, making it a workable choice for a native or dry-shade foundation planting as well as a straightforward container shrub.

planting.note: Site in lean soil with little summer water once established, choosing a sunny to lightly shaded spot that mimics its native eastern Mediterranean hillsides.

directions: Native to the eastern Mediterranean, this is one of the few evergreen to semi-evergreen maples, holding leathery dark green leaves that are either simple or three-lobed year-round in milder winters. Inconspicuous yellow flowers open in spring against the dark foliage, and the bark ages from smooth dark gray in youth to a scaly, fissured texture on older wood. Expect a slow-growing small tree or large shrub to roughly twenty feet tall and eight to ten feet wide, hardy to about minus ten Fahrenheit and needing only lean soil and minimal summer irrigation once it is established.

planting.note: Site in lean, fast-draining soil and water sparingly through the first summer only, then let it dry out completely in subsequent years for best form and bark color.

directions: This selection of the rare white-leaved manzanita was found near Ashland, Oregon, and stands out for its round, powdery pale blue-gray leaves and fiery orange-red new growth each spring. Clusters of pink-tinged white flowers open January through March ahead of the foliage flush. Give it neglected, unimproved ground rather than rich garden soil, since overwatering or fertile beds shorten its life considerably. It shows some deer resistance and tolerates heat well once established.

planting.note: Plant into gritty, sharply drained soil and expect only a few inches of growth per year, so place it where its eventual 3x3-foot dome won't need to be rushed.

directions: A naturally occurring Colorado hybrid manzanita prized for dense, dark matte-green foliage and trunks that exfoliate to a glossy maroon as the plant ages. Pink flower clusters fade to pale pink and are followed by russet-red berries. Water only to get the plant established, after which it should rely entirely on natural rainfall; this is one of the most cold-tolerant manzanitas available, shrugging off deep winter cold that would kill many California relatives. Patience is required since mature form takes close to a decade to develop.

planting.note: Site near a warm wall or in a sheltered urban garden spot, since this form is slightly less cold-hardy than the wild species.

directions: Found near Canberra, Australia, this grevillea selection carries gray-green foliage and rusty-orange buds that open to bright fresh orange in pendant winter clusters. It is a fast grower that can reach 8 feet in both directions, making it best suited to larger borders or as a loose screen. Water during the first season to establish roots, then taper to roughly monthly irrigation through summer drought. Its mild-season flowering is a strong draw for wintering Anna's hummingbirds in Pacific Northwest gardens.

planting.note: Plant in full sun for the most compact habit and heaviest bloom; part shade produces lankier growth with fewer flowers.

directions: This needle-leaved grevillea is noted by the nursery as one of the cold-hardiest cultivars of the species, surviving temperatures down to 5°F. Curling orange 'spider' flowers appear year-round on mature plants but peak heavily in spring, drawing hummingbirds. The foliage is genuinely sharp to the touch, so site it away from paths and foot traffic. Once roots are established it shrugs off drought with exceptional ease, growing into a broad low mound within about six years.

common_name: Blue Mountains Groundcover Grevillea (Red Toothbrush Flowers)

planting.note: Protect young plants below 15°F and reserve this one for the mildest microclimates in the garden; it is a true prostrate groundcover, not an upright shrub.

directions: A naturally occurring hybrid discovered in Australia's Blue Mountains, grown for oak-shaped leaves that emerge deep red and mature to green, plus upward-facing red 'toothbrush' flowers that appear mainly February through August. It stays under a foot tall while spreading up to 8 feet wide after about seven years, making it a striking slow-motion groundcover for a hot, dry slope. A little summer water speeds up its spread, but it is fundamentally drought-adapted once rooted in. The nursery flags it as hard to find, so it is a genuine rarity even among Grevillea collectors.

common_name: Angel's Fishing Rod 'Xera's Darkest Shades' (Deep Magenta Bells)

planting.note: Give it open ground with no competing plants nearby, and never cut the foliage back hard, since the evergreen leaves resent disturbance.

directions: A Xera-raised selection of the South African wandflower grown for unusually dark purple-to-magenta bell flowers held on gracefully arching wands above gray-green evergreen foliage. Plants bloom May through July and tower well above the 3-4 foot foliage clump when in flower. Keep soil rich and well drained, water generously through the growing season and bloom, then ease off once flowering finishes. It is highly deer resistant and, once sited, is best left completely undisturbed for years.

planting.note: Allow plenty of overhead room for the towering flower wands and resist moving or dividing the clump once it settles in.

directions: Called by the nursery the easiest and hardiest of the Angel's Fishing Rods, this cultivar sends up gracefully arching 8-foot wands hung with hot magenta tubular flowers in early summer above evergreen gray-blue foliage. It spreads slowly by offsets and is propagated only by division, so availability is limited. Regular summer water produces the best bloom, though established clumps tolerate drier conditions. Its sheer flower-stalk height makes it a dramatic focal point at the back of a sunny border.

planting.note: Give it rich, well-drained soil and regular summer water while young roots establish, then expect it to behave as a low-water plant thereafter.

directions: A South African relative of the thistle family grown for large, 4-inch daisy flowers in pale purple to white with a darker center for contrast. The ridged, spiny stems and foliage give it a slightly menacing architectural presence that discourages deer browsing. It dies back to a basal clump each winter and re-emerges slowly from a spreading crown. Site it where its thorny texture won't brush against walkways, and treat it as a low-water perennial once past its first season.

common_name: Honey Bush 'Antonow's Blue' (Giant Blue Pinnate Foliage)

planting.note: If top growth freezes to the ground in a hard winter, cut it back and expect vigorous regrowth from the established root system once soil warms.

directions: This blue-leaved honey bush cultivar is grown primarily for its enormous, deeply cut, glaucous-blue pinnate leaves that lend a bold, almost tropical presence to borders. After mild winters it also sends up tall flower spikes of unusual madder-red bracts hiding near-black flowers. It wants well-drained soil and regular summer water while it builds its size, though mature plants tolerate some drought. Expect it to reach roughly 7 feet tall and wide where winters stay above the mid-teens.

planting.note: Tuck into rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in part shade where slugs and snails are less of a threat than they are to most tender perennials.

directions: A little-known perennial hybrid forming tidy evergreen rosettes of fleshy, scalloped green leaves that stay attractive through all four seasons. From February into June it sends up compact 10-inch spikes of violet-blue tubular flowers, an unusually long and early bloom window for a woodland perennial. It thrives in the humus-rich, part-shaded conditions typical of Pacific Northwest gardens and shrugs off the slug and snail pressure that plagues many shade perennials. Plant it where its low, carefree mound can be viewed up close along a shaded path edge.

planting.note: Plant near sturdy neighbors for light support, since the lax stems tend to lean, and keep soil rich and evenly moist rather than letting it dry out in summer.

directions: A curious member of the carrot family from Mexico, grown for clumps of blue-toned, divided evergreen foliage and odd acid-green, cup-shaped flowers arranged in circular inflorescences each spring. It prefers part shade to full shade and modest summer moisture over the hot, bright conditions most carrot-family relatives tolerate. Only a male clone circulates in US cultivation, so plants never set seed and must be propagated by division. Its sprawling habit means it often leans into companions rather than standing fully upright, which can be used deliberately in a mixed shade bed.
